heading: PROPHET AL-YASAʿ (AS)
title: HONOURED BY ALLAH: THE GOODNESS THAT CONTINUES
themes: Guidance • Excellence • Humility • Truth • Service • Fairness • Remembering Allah
scope: 8 CONNECTED STORIES | 12 INTERACTIVE MISSIONS | 2 PRIMARY QUR’ANIC VERSES
reviewNote: Editorial working edition: all Qur’anic Arabic, translations, Tafsīr and child-safeguarding require independent final review.
introduction: Volume Nineteen continues our journey after Prophet Ilyās (AS). The Qur’an names al-Yasaʿ (AS) in al-Anʿām 6:86 among those whom Allah favoured, and in Ṣād 38:48 among the excellent. In classical Muslim scholarship he is recognised as a Prophet. The Qur’an does not narrate his childhood, a specific public sermon, the details of his relationship with Ilyās, a miracle, a named city, or the circumstances of his death. This volume therefore honours what is known instead of trying to invent a detailed biography.

The connected modern fiction follows Imaan, Akhlaq, Mohsin, Mohsina and the adults around them as they prepare a “Goodness That Continues” school exhibition. Their small everyday choices offer ethical applications of reverence, reliable learning, humble service and guidance. These fictional events must never be mistaken for historical events in al-Yasaʿ’s life. The general ethical themes are pedagogical applications informed by wider Islamic teaching, not specific deeds attributed to this Prophet.

stories.title: The Name on the Missing Bookmark
stories.subtitle: A name deserves evidence, not an invented adventure

blocks.text: After the lesson about Prophet Ilyās (AS), Akhlaq expected another thick folder of adventures. Instead, Dadi Jaan found a narrow green bookmark tucked into Sheikh Uncle’s Qur’an stand. It carried a single name: AL-YASAʿ. Underneath were two references: al-Anʿām 6:86 and Ṣād 38:48. ‘Only two?’ Akhlaq asked. ‘Two verses are enough to teach us something important,’ Dadi replied. Imaan carefully opened the Qur’an and read the references with her. The passages named al-Yasaʿ among people Allah honoured and among the excellent. Akhlaq searched a shelf and found a colourful children’s booklet. It told a lengthy story about a city and an extraordinary adventure. ‘Can we use this for our project?’ he asked. Sheikh Uncle read the pages. ‘We must first know which details come from the Qur’an, which come from later historical reports and which may be the writer’s imagination.’ Akhlaq looked disappointed. The school had announced a new exhibition, and the other groups were planning dramatic displays. Imaan suggested another kind of mystery: instead of pretending to know every missing detail, they would discover what Allah had actually told them. At home, Salaam drew three columns on a sheet: QUR’AN STATES, LATER SOURCE NEEDS REVIEW, and OUR FICTIONAL LESSON. They placed the bookmark in the first column. For once the unfinished story was not a problem to hide. It was a chance to learn care and honesty. Akhlaq wrote beneath the name: ‘A little knowledge should make me careful, not boastful.’

blocks.label: CARRY FORWARD
blocks.text: Begin with the evidence; do not fill gaps with attractive guesses.

stories.title: Two Verses, A Great Honour
stories.subtitle: Greatness is not measured by the number of stories

blocks.text: The next morning, Mohsin arrived carrying an enormous cardboard castle. ‘Every Prophet’s display needs something spectacular,’ he declared. Akhlaq loved the idea, but Imaan asked which Qur’anic verse described a castle belonging to al-Yasaʿ. None of them could find one. In their lesson, Sir Zameer read al-Anʿām 6:86 and Ṣād 38:48. ‘Allah honoured this Prophet,’ he said. ‘That is the firm truth. We should not treat a person as less important because the Qur’an gives fewer details about his individual life.’ Mohsina wrote the phrase CHOSEN BY ALLAH at the top of the poster. Akhlaq suggested ranking the Prophets according to how many verses named them. Sir Zameer gently stopped him. ‘The Prophets’ status is not measured by our number of flashcards. Allah knows their true ranks.’ The group set the castle aside and made two beautiful source panels. One displayed the meaning of Allah’s favour. The other displayed the description ‘among the excellent.’ At recess, a younger child approached the poster and asked what al-Yasaʿ had looked like. Imaan answered, ‘We do not know from these verses, and we will not make up his appearance.’ The child seemed satisfied and asked what they could learn instead. ‘That Allah honours His chosen servants,’ said Akhlaq, ‘and that we should learn His words carefully.’ He realised the display did not need a castle to be meaningful. The two verses already carried dignity greater than their decorations could provide.

blocks.label: CARRY FORWARD
blocks.text: Honour what Allah honours without pretending to know the unseen.

stories.title: The Unfinished Family Exhibition
stories.subtitle: Small helpful work can hold a team together

blocks.text: Team Amanah was given the least popular task at Sheikh Uncle’s Academy: arranging the exhibition’s source labels and cleaning the reading corner. Mohsin wanted to move the models; Akhlaq wanted to welcome guests; neither wanted to sort paper. Mohsina noticed that several labels had been placed beside the wrong displays. Visitors would read the incorrect information if nobody corrected them. Imaan remembered how the Qur’an had taught them to respect the names of Allah’s honoured servants. Their task was ordinary, not a reenactment of al-Yasaʿ’s life. Still, it was an opportunity to practise careful service. ‘People need accurate labels,’ she said. They agreed to divide the work. Mohsin carried boxes, Mohsina checked references, Imaan read the labels aloud and Akhlaq set them in place. Before lunch, a younger pupil tripped over a loose cable near the display. No one was hurt, but the team called the teacher and asked for the cable to be secured. The finished corner looked simple, yet it was safe and useful. Akhlaq discovered that a job did not become worthless because it was out of sight. Salaam visited after school and noticed a neat sign: PLEASE CHECK A SOURCE BEFORE SHARING A CLAIM. ‘Who made that?’ he asked. ‘All of us,’ Akhlaq said. He was pleased that the answer was true. The team had built something more lasting than one person’s moment in the spotlight: a place where visitors could learn reliably.

blocks.label: CARRY FORWARD
blocks.text: Choose beneficial work and share credit fairly.

stories.title: The Rumour with a Beautiful Cover
stories.subtitle: A pleasing story still requires careful checking

blocks.text: An attractive poster appeared on the class noticeboard. It claimed that the Qur’an described an astonishing event in the life of Prophet al-Yasaʿ. The artwork was excellent; the reference at the bottom was wrong. A group of students had already begun repeating the story. Akhlaq liked the picture so much that he nearly copied it into the school booklet. Imaan asked him to open the verse first. When they checked the reference, the named event was not there. ‘Maybe the artist had another source,’ Mohsin suggested. Sir Zameer encouraged them to ask politely rather than accusing the student of lying. The artist admitted that she had heard the story online and had not checked it. ‘I thought it sounded familiar,’ she said. ‘And I worked hard on the picture.’ Akhlaq understood how hard it was to remove something beautiful after spending so long making it. Together they redesigned the poster. It now included the verified words of the Qur’an about al-Yasaʿ, with a note that other details required scholarly checking. The painting was moved to a separate creative-art folder, without being presented as the Prophet’s life. During lunch Mohsin asked why accurate attribution mattered so much. Imaan replied, ‘Because a made-up detail may be repeated until people think Allah told us something He did not tell us.’ Nobody laughed at the artist. She thanked them for helping her correct the poster. In his notebook Akhlaq wrote: ‘Truth must decide the label, not the beauty of the cover.’

blocks.label: CARRY FORWARD
blocks.text: Check claims kindly, especially when the topic is sacred.

stories.title: The Quiet Helper
stories.subtitle: Serve without making other people feel small

blocks.text: The exhibition opened on a busy afternoon. A visitor arrived using a walking aid. The aisle near the source library was partly blocked by a table. Mohsina noticed first and asked Sir Zameer whether they could move it. Mohsin held the display board while Akhlaq helped clear the path. Nobody announced their names over the microphone. A little later, Akhlaq heard another student boasting that he had made the entire venue accessible. He was tempted to interrupt and list all the people who had helped. Dadi Jaan, who had witnessed their work, asked him a quieter question: ‘Would the visitor’s journey become less comfortable if no one praised you?’ Akhlaq shook his head. They sat at the source booth and returned to the Qur’anic phrase ‘among the excellent.’ Dadi explained that Allah’s praise of al-Yasaʿ was revelation. It was not a claim that this particular school action was something the Prophet had done. ‘We cannot award divine honour with a scoreboard,’ she added, ‘but we can make the choices before us useful and respectful.’ Akhlaq watched Mohsina ask the visitor whether the new path was convenient rather than assuming what they needed. He admired her thoughtfulness. At the end of the day, when the teacher invited each group to describe its work, Akhlaq thanked the entire team. He did not feel smaller for sharing the credit. He felt more connected to the others.

blocks.label: CARRY FORWARD
blocks.text: Help thoughtfully and recognise the contributions of others.

Sir Zameer announced that two volunteers would help younger pupils during the exhibition’s final session. Akhlaq immediately wrote Mohsin’s name at the top of the list, even though he had not asked whether Mohsin was available. Another child, who was usually quiet, had already offered to volunteer. ‘But Mohsin is my friend,’ Akhlaq protested when Imaan pointed this out. The teacher asked the class to choose according to availability, ability and the needs of the task, rather than popularity. Akhlaq felt embarrassed. His friendship mattered, but it did not give him permission to ignore someone else’s offer. He apologised and helped make a fair schedule so both could contribute at suitable times. Later, the class read al-Anʿām 6:86 again. Sheikh Uncle reminded them that Allah’s favour to the Prophets belongs to His knowledge and choosing; human beings must not turn that truth into arbitrary rankings of classmates. Their school example concerned ordinary fairness, not the divine selection of Prophets. At home, Akhlaq asked Salaam whether choosing his friends first was always wrong. Salaam answered that friendship is good, but entrusted decisions require justice. A teacher choosing a responsible helper must consider the duty. A child choosing a playmate may consider friendship. Akhlaq liked the distinction. The next morning, he wrote on the noticeboard: ‘For a shared duty, choose fairly and explain kindly.’

blocks.label: CARRY FORWARD
blocks.text: Do not let personal preference defeat a shared responsibility.

stories.title: The Correction Nobody Wanted
stories.subtitle: Admitting an error can restore trust

blocks.text: When the final proofs for the class booklet arrived, Imaan found a mistake in the spelling of al-Yasaʿ’s name and an incorrect reference under one verse. The printing deadline was near. Akhlaq groaned. ‘If we stop now, everyone will be upset.’ Mohsina said, ‘If we print it wrong, children may memorise the mistake.’ They took the proof to Sir Zameer, who thanked them for checking. He explained that Qur’anic text and attribution needed careful review before printing. The team sent a corrected draft to the school office. For an hour, Akhlaq worried that the whole booklet would be cancelled. Instead, the office returned a new proof with the references fixed. The pupils learned that correction was not a humiliation; it was a part of responsibility. At the closing assembly, another team was praised for submitting first. Akhlaq resisted the urge to argue that accuracy should be more important than speed. He thanked them, then showed his own team a short checklist they could use in the future. Dadi Jaan wrote three headings on his page: CHECK, CORRECT, CONTINUE. ‘People make mistakes,’ she said. ‘The danger is not always the first mistake. Sometimes it is refusing to correct what we now know is wrong.’ Akhlaq placed the corrected booklet next to the original green bookmark. Both carried the same name, now treated with greater care.

blocks.label: CARRY FORWARD
blocks.text: Correct errors without shame or blame, and learn from the process.

stories.title: What Shall We Carry Forward?
stories.subtitle: A legacy grows through faithful choices

blocks.text: The final afternoon at the academy was calm. The exhibition boards had been taken down, and the children sat in a circle with the cards they had collected. Imaan held the two-source bookmark. Mohsin held the teamwork checklist. Mohsina held the accessibility plan, and Akhlaq held the corrected booklet. Sheikh Uncle asked what they had learned about Prophet al-Yasaʿ. No one tried to invent a dramatic ending. Imaan answered carefully: ‘The Qur’an names him among those Allah favoured and among the excellent.’ ‘And what about his life?’ Sheikh Uncle asked. ‘The two verses do not give a full biography,’ said Mohsin. ‘So we should not pretend they do.’ Dadi Jaan reminded them that the modern stories had taught practical applications, but were not scenes from sacred history. Then she asked what they would choose to carry forward. Mohsina promised to notice when someone needed practical access or help. Imaan chose to check sources before teaching younger children. Mohsin chose to share credit and listen. Akhlaq paused before answering. ‘I want to learn without pretending I already know everything.’ Dadi smiled. ‘That is a valuable beginning.’ They made a final sign for the reading corner: HONOUR ALLAH’S WORDS. BE FAIR. DO GOOD. KEEP LEARNING. The compass stayed still beside the folder. No mystery door appeared. The next world would come in its proper time. For now, they had enough to practise in their homes, school and friendships.

blocks.label: CARRY FORWARD
blocks.text: Respect revelation and make useful, humble choices every day.

synthesis.text: What the Qur’an tells us about al-Yasaʿ (AS)

Allah explicitly names al-Yasaʿ in two places. In al-Anʿām 6:86, he is included with Ismāʿīl, Yūnus and Lūṭ among those whom Allah favoured. In Ṣād 38:48, he is mentioned alongside Ismāʿīl and Dhū al-Kifl as among the excellent. These statements are certain Qur’anic foundations. The detailed chronology and conversations often found in retellings are not supplied by these verses. We honour the Prophet through true remembrance rather than invented spectacle.
Eight things to carry forward
Remember the Prophets respectfully and accurately.
Do not mistake an attractive story for a verified source.
Distinguish sacred history from present-day fictional examples.
Be humble when knowledge is limited.
Help with useful work even when it attracts little attention.
Share credit fairly and avoid favouritism in entrusted duties.
Correct errors gently and accept corrections graciously.
Turn lessons into small voluntary everyday acts of goodness.
Seven-day family character practice
Day
Voluntary daily action
Private question
Read one primary verse with a caregiver
What exactly did the verse say?
Check a reference before repeating it
Was I certain or guessing?
Do one helpful household duty
Did I serve willingly?
Praise a friend’s real helpful action
Did I avoid judging their heart?
Choose fairly for one shared task
Did I favour anyone unfairly?
Correct a mistake with kindness
Did I protect dignity?
Review two Qur’anic references and choose one lasting action
What will I keep practising?
Final learning checks

Knowledge: identify 6:86 and 38:48; explain the expressions of divine favour and excellence; separate an explicit Qur’anic statement from an invented biography; recognise the limited scope of these verses. Character: make a safe and fair decision in a modern situation; explain it without comparing children’s faith. Learners may select Skip on any personal reflection.

Final family conversation: “What did Allah tell us directly?” “Which details must we not invent?” “How can helpful actions remain sincere even when nobody is watching?” “What should we do if we discover an error?” Parents should listen without publicly ranking children or demanding disclosures.
FINAL CARRY FORWARD • Honour the words Allah revealed. Admit what we do not know. Practise fairness, useful service and humble learning.
